title: The Tower and the Gyre: Yeats from the Pollexfen Water to Drumcliff
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Sandymount, Georgeville: the birth of a painter's son
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats). The house is Georgeville on Sandymount Avenue, rented by his father; a research claim that it belonged to his maternal grandparents is wrong, since the Pollexfens lived at Merville in Sligo.
stops.campa: In a rented house on Sandymount Avenue, two miles from the centre of Dublin, a first child is born to John Butler Yeats, a barrister abandoning law for painting, and Susan Pollexfen, daughter of a Sligo shipping family who will never be reconciled to any city. They call him William Butler after the clerical grandfathers of his line. His father's people are Church of Ireland parsons and lawyers who talk for a living, and who leave canvases unfinished. His mother's own ships at Sligo and say almost nothing at table.
suggested_refs: Georgeville, 5 Sandymount Avenue, Dublin 4, the birthplace
sources: R. F. Foster, W. B. Yeats: A Life I (1997)

stops.name: Merville, Sligo: the summers in the merchant house
stops.date_confidence: the Sligo summers run roughly 1868 to 1880 in the biographical accounts; no single arrival date is documented, and month and day are defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Every summer the children are shipped west to their grandfather's house above the Garavogue, a merchant's place of mills, warehouses and steamers, where William Pollexfen rules his household like a captain and his grandson watches him with terror and admiration together. The boy who cannot learn to read in London learns the name of every boat in the harbour here, and gets from the servants the stories of the fairy people and the second sight. He says for the rest of his life that Sligo is his home, and he never once lives there as a man.
suggested_refs: Merville, the Pollexfen house at Sligo, and Reveries over Childhood and Youth (1916)
sources: Yeats, Reveries over Childhood and Youth (1916)

stops.name: Rosses Point: the pilots and the drowned
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the boyhood visits are dated to the 1870s in general terms only, and the year here is the middle of that span rather than a documented date
stops.campa: At the point where the Garavogue meets the sea his Pollexfen uncles keep pilot boats, and the boy sails and fishes among men who count the drowned by name. He gathers what he hears: the fairy country under Knocknarea, the woman taken and given back, the lights moving on the water at night. Years afterward he prints these stories in London as The Celtic Twilight and is accused of inventing them. He is not inventing them. He is repeating, in a printing house four hundred miles away, what pilots told a boy nobody thought clever.
suggested_refs: Rosses Point, Co. Sligo, and Yeats, The Celtic Twilight (1893)

stops.name: Benbulbin: the mountain that does not move
stops.date_confidence: the mountain belongs to the whole childhood and to the last poem; the year is a placeholder inside the Sligo summers and is not a documented date. Coordinate corrected to the summit at 54 deg 22 min N, 8 deg 28 min W; a research figure of 54.381, -8.4402 sits over two kilometres off the mountain.
stops.campa: North of the town a limestone table stands over the plain with its sides cut sheer, seventeen hundred feet of it, the mountain under which Diarmuid was killed by the boar in the old story. It closes every horizon of his childhood. He will spend his sixties building a system in which history runs in cones and every civilisation is undone by its opposite. In the last year of his life he writes a poem naming this mountain and leaves instructions to be buried in its shadow.
suggested_refs: Benbulbin, Co. Sligo, and Yeats, Under Ben Bulben (1938)

stops.name: Bedford Park, Chiswick: the artists' suburb
stops.date_confidence: the family lived at 8 Woodstock Road in Bedford Park 1879 to 1881 and at 3 Blenheim Road from 1888; month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the Bedford Park estate, 51.5001, -0.2617; a research figure of 51.4949, -0.2777 falls outside it.
stops.campa: The father moves his family into a new suburb west of London built for artists, red brick and Queen Anne gables, where painters keep open house and nobody works to a clock. The boy is sent to the Godolphin School in Hammersmith and does badly there, better at cricket and at daydreaming than at Latin, mocked for an Irish accent. In the studio his father reads him Balzac and Shelley aloud and tells him that a man is made by passion and not by opinion. He is failing Latin at school and being read Shelley at home, and it is the reading at home that takes.
suggested_refs: 8 Woodstock Road and 3 Blenheim Road, Bedford Park, London W4

stops.name: Erasmus Smith High School, Harcourt Street: the return to Dublin
stops.date_confidence: the family returned to Dublin at the end of 1880 and Yeats entered the Erasmus Smith High School in October 1881; a research claim dating the return itself to 1881 is off by a few months
stops.campa: The father's money runs out and the family goes back to Ireland; from the school on Harcourt Street the boy walks each day past the shuttered Georgian fronts of a capital that has no parliament sitting in it. Here he reads Irish legend seriously for the first time, the Ossianic cycle and the heroes Standish O'Grady has begun putting into English, and sees what has not been made: a literature for a country that exists mainly as memory. He is a poor student, and he leaves school without sitting for Trinity, where his father and his grandfather went.
suggested_refs: The Erasmus Smith High School, Harcourt Street, Dublin

stops.name: Metropolitan School of Art, Kildare Street: painting and George Russell
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats); month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Instead of Trinity he enters the art school on Kildare Street, because his father's trade is painting and painting is the one profession the household understands. He is a mediocre draughtsman. He finds there George Russell, a boy who sees visions and does not consider this remarkable, and the two of them spend the life classes talking about Theosophy. Within two years the pair of them are running a society for the study of hidden matters, and Yeats has stopped pretending that he intends to paint.
suggested_refs: The Metropolitan School of Art, Kildare Street, Dublin

stops.name: York Street, Dublin: the Hermetic Society founded
stops.date_confidence: the founding is dated to June 1885 by Foster and by Yeats's Autobiographies; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: In rooms on York Street he and a handful of friends found the Dublin Hermetic Society and put him in the chair, a body constituted against scientific materialism and for whatever might survive it: Theosophy, the Upanishads, the reports of the psychical researchers. Mohini Chatterjee comes from India that year to lecture a Dublin lodge, and the young men question him closely about rebirth and about what remains when desire is gone. Yeats is twenty. He keeps this study for the next fifty-four years, and it outlasts every order he joins.
suggested_refs: The Dublin Hermetic Society, June 1885, and Mohini Chatterjee's Dublin lectures

stops.name: Holland Park, 17 Lansdowne Road: Blavatsky's household
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The house is attested as Blavatsky's from 1887 and as the address The Secret Doctrine was published from in October 1888; Yeats's introduction, his membership of the Esoteric Section and the account of his expulsion after demanding experimental tests are standard biography that could not be confirmed in the encyclopedia sources reachable here. Coordinate inherited unchanged from blavatsky.journey.json.
stops.campa: In a house in Holland Park the old Russian sits smoking at a card table and receives the occult traffic of an empire, and from these rooms in October she publishes The Secret Doctrine, two volumes claiming to translate a book that no library holds. Yeats comes to Blavatsky as a young Irishman with fairy stories and a proposal: that the powers be tested, that phenomena be put to an experiment and written up. The Esoteric Section is not a laboratory. He is out of it within a couple of years, and inside the Golden Dawn by the March after that.
suggested_refs: 17 Lansdowne Road, Holland Park, Blavatsky's London household and the Esoteric Section

stops.name: Lough Gill: the lake isle written in a London street
stops.date_confidence: the composition is dated 1888 and the poem was published in 1890; no adult visit to the islet is documented, and month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: On a London pavement he passes a shop window with a small fountain balancing a ball on its jet, and the sound of the water brings back an islet in a Sligo lake and a boyhood plan to live there alone in a hut of clay and wattles, as Thoreau had lived. He writes twelve lines that will be recited by people who have never crossed the Irish Sea. He never builds the cabin. The island stays empty, half an acre of trees in a lake, and the poem is printed in 1890 without his having gone back to look at the place.
suggested_refs: The Lake Isle of Innisfree, Lough Gill, Co. Sligo
sources: Yeats, The Lake Isle of Innisfree (1890)

stops.name: Bedford Park, 3 Blenheim Road: Maud Gonne at the door
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested (Wikipedia, Maud Gonne); the day, 30 January 1889, is Foster's and is the standard biographical date. The call was at the Yeats family house at 3 Blenheim Road; a research entry inventing a separate Woodstock Road studio pin is set aside.
stops.campa: A cab stops outside the family house in Bedford Park and Maud Gonne comes up the path with a letter of introduction from John O'Leary: an heiress turned revolutionary, six feet of her, an actress who has given up the stage for Ireland. Yeats is twenty-three. He records afterwards that the troubling of his life began. He proposes in 1891 and is refused, and proposes again, and again; in 1916 he asks her for the last time, and when she refuses he asks her daughter Iseult, who refuses too.
suggested_refs: 3 Blenheim Road, Bedford Park, and Yeats, Memoirs

stops.name: Isis-Urania Temple, Mark Masons' Hall: Demon Est Deus Inversus
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats); the day, 7 March 1890, comes from R. A. Gilbert's Golden Dawn Companion. The temple's meeting hall is given as Mark Masons' Hall at Great Queen Street in one source and at 33 Golden Square, Soho, in another; the pin follows Great Queen Street and the contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: In a hired masonic hall he is initiated into the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn and takes the motto Demon Est Deus Inversus, the devil is God inverted. The ladder of grades he starts to climb was cut from the Societas Rosicruciana, which grew out of the Rosicrucian appetite that Bulwer-Lytton's Zanoni had fed a generation earlier. He is at this time editing William Blake with Edwin Ellis, three volumes on a prophet nobody has yet explained. The symbolism of the grades and the symbolism of Blake are, for him, one study.
stops.quote: If I had not made magic my constant study I could not have written a single word of my Blake book, nor would The Countess Kathleen ever have come to exist. The mystical life is the centre of all that I do and all that I think and all that I write.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, letter of 1892, quoted in Richard Ellmann, Yeats: The Man and the Masks (1948), p. 97
suggested_refs: Golden Dawn Isis-Urania membership rolls for March 1890, not consulted
sources: R. A. Gilbert, The Golden Dawn Companion

stops.name: Woburn Buildings, Bloomsbury: the Monday evenings
stops.date_confidence: the tenancy ran 1895 to 1919 (Wikipedia, Woburn Walk); a research entry giving 1896 to 1919 is corrected here. The address is 18 Woburn Buildings before renumbering and 5 Woburn Walk after, one door under two names. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He takes a narrow set of rooms above a shop off the Euston Road and keeps them for twenty-four years, through the Order, the theatre and both refusals. On Monday evenings the door stands open: Arthur Symons, the young men of the Rhymers' Club, later an American in a velvet jacket making the tea and correcting his host's diction. The rooms are dark, hung with prints, badly heated, and lit by candles because he prefers them. It is the only address in London at which he can reliably be found.
suggested_refs: 18 Woburn Buildings, now 5 Woburn Walk, Bloomsbury

stops.name: Kelmscott Press, 14 Upper Mall: the most beautiful book of the age
stops.date_confidence: the Kelmscott Chaucer was finished at the press in June 1896; coordinate inherited unchanged from edward_burne_jones.journey.json
stops.campa: At the press on Upper Mall by the river, William Morris finishes the Chaucer he has spent four years making, with eighty-seven woodcuts drawn by Edward Burne-Jones and borders that leave the page no rest. Yeats calls it the most beautiful book of the age. Six years later his sisters set up a press of their own at Dundrum on Morris's method, Dun Emer and afterwards Cuala, and begin printing their brother's books by hand on Irish paper, in a single type, unillustrated.
suggested_refs: The Kelmscott Chaucer, finished June 1896, Kelmscott Press, Hammersmith

stops.name: Isis-Urania, London: whether the Order is to remain a magical order
stops.date_confidence: the revolt against Mathers is 1900, triggered by his initiating Aleister Crowley at the Paris temple on 16 January 1900; the pamphlet Is the Order of R. R. & A. C. to Remain a Magical Order? was privately printed by Yeats in 1901. A research entry merging both into 1900 and adding a resignation is wrong: he stayed on, and remained in the successor order Stella Matutina until 1921. Month and day of the pamphlet unrecorded.
stops.campa: The chief in Paris initiates a young man named Crowley whom London will not accept, and the temple revolts against Mathers; Crowley comes to take the vault by force and is put out. Yeats, thirty-five and running the ritual side of the house, prints a pamphlet at his own cost asking whether the Order is to remain a magical order at all, which is his way of asking whether the ceremonies do anything. Arthur Edward Waite, initiated ten months after him, has already decided they are literature with a good pedigree.
suggested_refs: Yeats, Is the Order of R. R. & A. C. to Remain a Magical Order? (privately printed, 1901)
sources: Wikipedia, Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn

segments.name: Coole, the Theatre, and the Gold Wall

stops.name: Coole Park, Gort: the copper beech
stops.date_confidence: the introduction by Edward Martyn and the first visit are dated 1896; the month is the summer of that year in the accounts and the day is not recorded. Coordinate corrected to the demesne centre at 53.0965, -8.835; a research figure of 53.0847, -8.8264 sits over a kilometre off and does not reproduce the attested three miles between Coole and Ballylee.
stops.campa: Edward Martyn brings him to Lady Augusta Gregory's demesne at Gort: seven miles of wood and water, a lake with swans on it, and a library. She is a widow of forty-four taking down the folklore of her tenants word for word. He is a poet of thirty-one with no money and a bad stomach. She feeds him, houses him every summer for the rest of her life, and hears the speech of the country better than he can. On the great copper beech he cuts his initials among the others she collects there.
suggested_refs: The autograph tree at Coole Park, Gort, Co. Galway

stops.name: Paris: Maud Gonne marries Major MacBride
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats); the marriage is dated to February 1903 in the standard accounts, but the pool carries the year alone, so month and day are defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In Paris, Maud Gonne marries John MacBride, the major who raised an Irish brigade to fight the British in the Transvaal, a man with the war record she has always said a husband of hers would need. Yeats learns of it and goes on with the theatre, the Order, the lectures and the letters to her. The marriage collapses inside two years and she does not come back to him. Thirteen years after that, MacBride is shot in a Dublin prison yard and walks into a Yeats poem as a lout who has been changed utterly.
suggested_refs: The marriage of Maud Gonne and John MacBride, Paris, February 1903

stops.name: Abbey Theatre, Lower Abbey Street: three one-act plays
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, Abbey Theatre). The opening bill was three one-act plays: Yeats's On Baile's Strand and Cathleen Ni Houlihan and Lady Gregory's Spreading the News; a research entry naming only two of the three is completed here.
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of December the theatre opens on Lower Abbey Street with three one-act plays: his own On Baile's Strand and Cathleen Ni Houlihan, and Lady Gregory's Spreading the News. Five years earlier he had founded the Irish Literary Theatre with Gregory, Martyn and George Moore on a subscription and a promise. He will direct and defend this house for the rest of his life, and in 1907 will stand on its stage in front of an audience rioting at Synge's Playboy of the Western World.
suggested_refs: The Abbey Theatre opening bill, 27 December 1904

stops.name: Basilica of San Vitale, Ravenna: the gold mosaic of a wall
stops.date_confidence: the Italian journey with Lady Gregory and Robert Gregory is dated to spring 1907 in Foster and in Yeats's letters of that year; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: Travelling through Italy with Lady Gregory and her son Robert, he stands in the dim brick octagon at Ravenna where Justinian and Theodora face each other across the apse in gold tesserae, an emperor and an empress made permanent by craftsmen who set each stone at a slight tilt so that the light would move across it. He is forty-one and has nothing to say about it yet. Two decades pass. The wall comes back as the wall the sages stand in, and an old man asks them to step out of it and teach him to sing.
stops.quote: O sages standing in God's holy fire / As in the gold mosaic of a wall, / Come from the holy fire, perne in a gyre, / And be the singing-masters of my soul. / Consume my heart away; sick with desire / And fastened to a dying animal / It knows not what it is; and gather me / Into the artifice of eternity.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, Sailing to Byzantium, stanza 3, in The Tower (1928); text as given by the Academy of American Poets
suggested_refs: The apse mosaics of San Vitale, Ravenna

stops.name: London, Woburn Buildings: Ezra Pound presents himself
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats); month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Ezra Pound arrives in London out of Idaho and Venice, twenty-three years old and certain that the greatest living poet in English is Irish, and presents himself. Yeats is forty-four and at the end of the Celtic manner, tired of his own adjectives and unable to get past them. Pound edits him without being asked, strikes out the vagueness, tells him his diction belongs in a museum. Yeats does not throw him out. Responsibilities appears in 1914 with the padding cut out of the line and a bitterness in it that none of the earlier books carry.
suggested_refs: The Monday evenings at Woburn Buildings and the Yeats and Pound correspondence

stops.name: Stone Cottage, Coleman's Hatch: the Noh in the winter forest
stops.date_confidence: the winters at Stone Cottage run 1913 to 1916; November is given as the start of the first winter rather than as a documented date, and the day is not recorded
stops.campa: For three winters the two men shut themselves into a cottage at the edge of Ashdown Forest, Pound acting as secretary for board and a small wage, reading aloud in the evenings from Ernest Fenollosa's papers: the Noh plays of Japan, a drama of masks and chorus, a bare stage, a musician folding and unfolding a cloth, and a dance at the climax where speech gives out. Yeats has been trying for twenty years to make a theatre that is rite rather than report. In January 1916 he drafts At the Hawk's Well.
suggested_refs: Stone Cottage, Coleman's Hatch, Sussex, and the Fenollosa Noh papers

stops.name: Dublin: Easter, 1916
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats); the poem is dated 25 September 1916 in the standard editions, but the pool carries the year alone, so month and day are defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Sixteen men are shot in a stone yard in Dublin over ten days in May, among them MacBride, who married Maud Gonne, and Pearse and MacDonagh, who wrote verses Yeats had read without much interest. He had thought them fools with pikes and had written mocking lines about the shopkeepers of the city. That summer he writes a poem which neither takes the judgment back nor repeats it, with a refrain about a terrible beauty, and then holds it out of print for four years while the country goes on burning.
suggested_refs: Yeats, Easter, 1916, dated 25 September 1916

stops.name: Ballylee, Co. Galway: a ruined tower for thirty-five pounds
stops.date_confidence: the source says he purchased it in 1916 or 1917 for thirty-five pounds; the price is firm and the year is not, so 1917 here stands for a disputed date rather than a settled one. Coordinate corrected to 53.1032, -8.7748; research figures of 53.1024, -8.8721 and 53.1244, -8.7847 place the pin six and two kilometres away respectively.
stops.campa: He buys a fifteenth-century de Burgo tower and the two cottages against its wall, four miles from Coole on the Streamstown river, for thirty-five pounds: roofless, floorless, a stone stair winding up the inside and water running under the foundation. He is fifty-one and has never owned a house, and he pays for this one out of lecture fees. The Normans built it, the de Burgos left it, and it stands in a country that within three years will be burning houses of exactly this kind, for what they are taken to mean.
stops.quote: An ancient bridge, and a more ancient tower, / A farmhouse that is sheltered by its wall.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, Meditations in Time of Civil War, II, My House, in The Tower (1928)
suggested_refs: Thoor Ballylee, near Gort, Co. Galway

stops.name: Harrow Road Register Office, London: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats)
stops.campa: Refused by Maud Gonne in the summer and by her daughter Iseult in the autumn, he marries Georgie Hyde-Lees at a register office on the Harrow Road with Ezra Pound standing as witness. She is twenty-five, he is fifty-two; his friends warn him about the gap and about the haste, and he agrees with them privately for a week. She has been in the Order for three years and has read more of its literature than most of its adepts, and nobody at the register office thinks to ask her about it. Four days later she picks up a pencil.
suggested_refs: The marriage register, Harrow Road Register Office, 20 October 1917

stops.name: Ashdown Forest Hotel, Forest Row: the automatic script begins
stops.date_confidence: the Wikipedia summary gives only the year; the first session is dated to 24 October 1917, four days after the wedding, in widely cited secondary accounts and in Foster
stops.campa: Four days married and wretched, convinced he has ruined two lives, he watches his wife take up a pencil and let her hand move without her attention. Words come. They answer, in a figure about the cat and the hare, the exact question tormenting him. He asks who is writing. Over the next three years the answer fills more than three thousand pages in her hand, dictated by voices that call themselves the Instructors and say plainly what they have come for: we have come to give you metaphors for poetry.
suggested_refs: The automatic script of George Yeats, begun 24 October 1917

stops.name: 4 Broad Street, Oxford: the gyres and the falcon
stops.date_confidence: the Oxford rooms are dated 1919 to 1922; month and day defaulted. The Second Coming was written in January 1919 and published in Michael Robartes and the Dancer (1920).
stops.campa: With George and their infant daughter he takes rooms on Broad Street and spends his days sorting the script into a system: twenty-eight phases of the moon, two cones running into each other point to base, one civilisation unwinding exactly as its opposite winds. Europe is climbing out of a war and Ireland is walking into one. In this house he writes the poem about the falcon that cannot hear the falconer and the beast that slouches towards Bethlehem, and reads it himself as a weather report rather than a prophecy.
stops.quote: Turning and turning in the widening gyre / The falcon cannot hear the falconer; / Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold; / Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, The Second Coming, in Michael Robartes and the Dancer (1920)
suggested_refs: 4 Broad Street, Oxford, and the manuscripts of The Second Coming

stops.name: Thoor Ballylee: the tower roofed and occupied
stops.date_confidence: disputed. Wikipedia's Thoor Ballylee article dates the restoration under the architect William A. Scott to 1921 to 1923 and the family's summer occupation to 1921 to 1929; Foster and most Yeats scholarship put the main work in 1917 to 1919, and Scott died in 1921. A research entry giving 1918 for the work and 1919 for the occupancy contradicts its own cited source. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Local masons reroof the tower with sea-green slates and old mill boards, cut wider windows into the lower floors, leave the narrow ones above as the Normans left them, and the family moves in for the summers. He works at a deal table on the first floor with the river running under the window and the stone stair going up into the dark above him. Nine summers here produce most of two books, and he puts the tower at the centre of both: a symbol a man can climb, and be cold in.
stops.quote: I declare this tower is my symbol; I declare / This winding, gyring, spiring treadmill of a stair is my ancestral stair; / That Goldsmith and the Dean, Berkeley and Burke have travelled there.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, Blood and the Moon, II, in The Winding Stair and Other Poems (1933)
suggested_refs: Thoor Ballylee, restored under William A. Scott, and the Yeats summer residences 1921 to 1929

stops.name: 82 Merrion Square, Dublin: gunfire in the square
stops.date_confidence: the family occupied the house 1922 to 1928; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The family takes a Georgian house on Merrion Square in the year the Free State is proclaimed and the men who made it begin shooting one another. A bomb goes off in the street. Irregulars and Free State soldiers exchange fire outside the windows while he works upstairs and his wife counts the holes in the glass afterwards. He is writing, in this house and in these months, a sequence about a house, a tower, an ancestral stair, and the road at the door where the men with rifles are standing.
suggested_refs: 82 Merrion Square, Dublin, the Yeats house 1922 to 1928

stops.name: Leinster House, Kildare Street: appointed senator
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats); reappointed 1925, term ending 1928. Coordinate corrected to the Kildare Street entrance at 53.3405, -6.2545; a research figure of 53.3403, -6.2513 lands on the Merrion Square side of the block.
stops.campa: He is appointed to the Senate of the Irish Free State on the eleventh of December, one of the nominated members meant to speak for a Protestant and unionist minority inside a state built by the men who fought it. He serves six years, sits on committees for manuscripts and for coinage, defends the theatre, argues against censorship, and speaks for a class the new order has no use for. Senators' houses are being burned that winter, and a guard is put on his door.
stops.quote: This country will not always be an uncomfortable place for a country gentleman to live in, and it is most important that we should keep in this country a certain leisured class.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, speech in Seanad Eireann, 28 March 1923
suggested_refs: Seanad Eireann debates, 1922 to 1928

stops.name: Stockholm, the Swedish Academy: the spirit of a whole nation
stops.date_confidence: the prize was announced on 14 November 1923 and conferred at Stockholm on 10 December 1923; a research entry dating the Stockholm event to November conflates announcement with ceremony
stops.campa: In Stockholm he takes the prize from the hand of the King of Sweden and gives a lecture called The Irish Dramatic Movement, in which he speaks less about his poems than about a theatre, and about two people not in the room: Lady Gregory, and John Synge, nine years dead. The money is close to eight thousand pounds and the first thing he does with it is pay his debts. He is being honoured, he notes, as the representative of a nation eleven months old.
stops.quote: for his always inspired poetry, which in a highly artistic form gives expression to the spirit of a whole nation
suggested_refs: Yeats, Nobel Lecture, The Irish Dramatic Movement (1923)

stops.name: Leinster House, Dublin: the coinage committee
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats); month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He takes the chair of the committee that is to design the new state's money and rules out the obvious: no portraits of ministers, no harps carrying slogans, no crosses. The designs that come back are animals. A horse, a salmon, a hare, a woodcock, a bull, cut clean and unlettered, and the country carries them in its pockets for the next seventy years. He is settling the look of the currency in the same building and the same years in which he is losing the argument about divorce.
stops.quote: elegant, racy of the soil, and utterly unpolitical
stops.quote_source: Yeats on the requirement set for the Irish Free State coinage committee, 1924
suggested_refs: The Irish Free State coinage of 1928 and the committee papers of 1924 to 1926

stops.name: Leinster House, Dublin: the divorce debate
stops.date_confidence: the speech is dated 11 June 1925; the Oireachtas official record at oireachtas.ie returned HTTP 403 and could not be checked directly, so the wording follows Foster, A Life II, p. 294 and Garratt (1989)
stops.campa: The government moves to make divorce impossible in the Free State, and he rises to tell a Catholic majority what it is doing to a Protestant minority and to any hope of the North ever coming in. He is abused in the newspapers for weeks and told he does not represent Ireland. He is representing precisely the people he was appointed to represent, and he names them from the floor: Swift, Berkeley, Burke, Grattan. The bill passes. The ban stays in Irish law until 1996.
stops.quote: We against whom you have done this thing, are no petty people. We are one of the great stocks of Europe.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, speech in Seanad Eireann, divorce debate, 11 June 1925, quoted in Robert F. Garratt, Modern Irish Poetry (1989) and Foster, A Life II, p. 294
suggested_refs: Seanad Eireann, official report of the divorce debate, 11 June 1925

stops.name: London: A Vision privately printed
stops.date_confidence: the title page is dated 1925 and the actual publication by T. Werner Laurie is January 1926; composition ran between Dublin, Oxford and Ballylee, and the pin is placed at Dublin rather than at the London imprint
stops.campa: The book made out of his wife's hand appears at last, privately printed in a small edition, dated 1925 on the title page and published in January of the year after: twenty-eight phases of the moon, the interpenetrating cones, the wheel on which every soul and every civilisation is set turning, and a chapter that reads two thousand years of history as one gyre giving way to its opposite. He will spend eleven more years rewriting it, and he never says in public whether it is true.
stops.quote: I dare say I delude myself in thinking this book my book of books.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, letter to his publisher T. Werner Laurie, early 1924, quoted in Foster, A Life II, p. 245
suggested_refs: A Vision, privately published by T. Werner Laurie, title page 1925, issued January 1926

stops.name: Cappella Palatina, Palermo: the second gold wall
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Foster, A Life II); month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Wintering in Sicily for his health he climbs to Roger's palace chapel, a room where Byzantine gold, an Arab honeycomb ceiling and a Norman king's throne occupy the same fifty feet without any of them apologising. This is the second such wall he has stood under. In his own system there is a moment near the year five hundred and fifty when religious, aesthetic and practical life were one thing, and a craftsman could work without being asked what he believed; the ceiling over his head is what he takes for evidence.
suggested_refs: The Norman and Byzantine mosaics of the Cappella Palatina, Palermo

stops.name: Thoor Ballylee: Sailing to Byzantium written
stops.date_confidence: the composition is dated 1926 and the poem first appeared in the Cuala Press collection October Blast in 1927, then in The Tower in 1928; a research entry calling October Blast a periodical is corrected here. Month and day defaulted; the place is given only as Ireland in the pool.
stops.campa: At sixty he writes the poem of an old man who leaves a country of salmon and mackerel and young lovers in one another's arms and sails to a city he has never seen. He explains it afterwards for a broadcast: Byzantium was the centre of European civilisation and the source of its spiritual philosophy, so the search for the spiritual life is symbolised by a journey to that city, and it is right for an old man to make his soul. The room he writes it in is a Norman ruin with a river under the floor.
stops.quote: An aged man is but a paltry thing, / A tattered coat upon a stick, unless / Soul clap its hands and sing, and louder sing / For every tatter in its mortal dress, / Nor is there singing school but studying / Monuments of its own magnificence; / And therefore I have sailed the seas and come / To the holy city of Byzantium.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, Sailing to Byzantium, stanza 2, in The Tower (1928); text as given by the Academy of American Poets
suggested_refs: October Blast (Cuala Press, 1927), first appearance of Sailing to Byzantium

stops.name: Byzantium: the city he does not go to
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Yeats never visited the city; the pin marks a destination that exists only in the poems and in A Vision, and the date is that of The Tower rather than of any journey. Coordinate inherited unchanged from constantino_el_grande.journey.json.
stops.campa: He never goes. The city on the Bosphorus is six days off and full of Turks with a republic a few years old, and he does not spend one of those days. What he sails to is a sixth-century capital assembled out of a Ravenna apse, a Palermo ceiling and a chapter of his own book, a place where craftsmen hammered gold birds that sing on a golden bough and no one signed the work. The voyage is out of the body and out of time. He is writing about Justinian's city, and the trains go to Istanbul.
stops.quote: Once out of nature I shall never take / My bodily form from any natural thing, / But such a form as Grecian goldsmiths make / Of hammered gold and gold enamelling / To keep a drowsy Emperor awake; / Or set upon a golden bough to sing / To lords and ladies of Byzantium / Of what is past, or passing, or to come.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, Sailing to Byzantium, stanza 4, in The Tower (1928); text as given by the Academy of American Poets
suggested_refs: A Vision, Dove or Swan, on Byzantium before Justinian
sources: Yeats, A Vision, Dove or Swan

stops.name: Dublin: The Tower published, the Senate and the tower left
stops.date_confidence: year attested for all three events (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats; Wikipedia, Thoor Ballylee): The Tower published, retirement from the Senate on grounds of ill health, and the last stay at Ballylee, with the family leaving for good in 1929. Months and days not recorded.
stops.campa: The Tower is published: the title poem, Sailing to Byzantium, Meditations in Time of Civil War, Nineteen Hundred and Nineteen. He is sixty-three, spitting blood, out of the Senate the same year on his doctors' orders, and he has just written the strongest book of his life. In the autumn he sees Ballylee for the last time. The family leaves it the following year, the river comes back in, and the roof he paid for with lecture money is gone inside a decade.
suggested_refs: Yeats, The Tower (1928)

stops.name: Rapallo, Liguria: the winters above the harbour
stops.date_confidence: attested as a run of winters from 1928 to 1934 (Foster, A Life II); month and day are not recorded and are defaulted to 01
stops.campa: For six winters he takes rooms above the harbour on the Ligurian coast, where Ezra Pound has settled with his cats and his arguments and where the sun costs nothing. His lungs are bad and the doctors here are agreeable. He writes much of The Winding Stair in these rooms and begins pulling A Vision apart for a second edition that will explain the system without the fiction he wrapped the first one in. Pound reads the new scheme and is unconvinced. They walk together every afternoon regardless.
suggested_refs: The Yeats winters at Rapallo, 1928 to 1934, and the composition of The Winding Stair

stops.name: London: the Steinach operation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats); performed by Norman Haire in London
stops.campa: At sixty-eight he goes to a London surgeon for the Steinach operation, a vasectomy sold across Europe as rejuvenation on the theory that closing the duct drives the gland's secretion back into the blood. The press gets hold of it and gives him a nickname he pretends not to have heard. Whatever the procedure does to an endocrine system, something happens to the work: the last five years produce Purgatory, the Last Poems, and a run of late attachments he takes no trouble to hide.
suggested_refs: Norman Haire and the Steinach rejuvenation operation, London, 6 April 1934

stops.name: Mallorca: the Upanishads with Shri Purohit Swami
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, W. B. Yeats); month and day not recorded. The pool names the island only, so the pin is placed at Palma, its capital, and the exact residence is unverified.
stops.campa: He sails to Mallorca with Shri Purohit Swami to put the principal Upanishads into English, an old Irishman and a Hindu monk working through Sanskrit in a Mediterranean winter, hunting a plain speech for the texts rather than a scholarly one. He nearly dies there of heart and kidney failure and his wife comes out to nurse him. The Ten Principal Upanishads appears in 1938 with both their names on it, the same year as his collected Autobiographies and the Abbey premiere of Purgatory.
suggested_refs: Yeats and Shri Purohit Swami, The Ten Principal Upanishads (1938)

stops.name: Hotel Ideal Sejour, Roquebrune-Cap-Martin: the death
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested to the day; the place is disputed. Wikipedia's Yeats article puts the Hotel Ideal Sejour in Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, while Wikipedia's Roquebrune-Cap-Martin article puts it in neighbouring Menton, and the two research lenses give coordinates a kilometre apart. This pin follows the afterlife figure; the Menton claim is not resolved.
stops.campa: The hotel stands on a stretch of coast road that Roquebrune and Menton have never quite agreed how to divide between them. He dies there of heart failure at seventy-three, with George beside him, three weeks after posting a letter to Lady Elizabeth Pelham that sets down what forty years of system-building came to. He has been correcting proofs and finishing poems until a few days before. The war is eight months away. The body will not be moved for nine years, and what is finally moved will be argued over for the rest of the century.
stops.quote: Man can embody truth but he cannot know it.
stops.quote_source: Yeats, letter to Lady Elizabeth Pelham, 4 January 1939
suggested_refs: The Hotel Ideal Sejour, on the Roquebrune and Menton boundary

stops.name: Roquebrune cemetery: the grave taken for a year
stops.date_confidence: the burial two days after death is attested; the coordinate is the Roquebrune commune centre, since a research figure of 43.7649, 7.4989 lies nearly three kilometres east, toward Menton
stops.campa: He is buried two days later in the village cemetery above the sea, at a small private funeral, in a grave taken on a term rather than in perpetuity. The instruction he leaves is exact: bury him here, and in a year, when the newspapers have forgotten him, take him up and put him in Sligo. In September the German army moves. The year becomes nine years, the concession on the grave lapses while nobody in Ireland can reach this coast, and the plot is cleared as the commune clears any plot.
suggested_refs: The cemetery of Roquebrune-Cap-Martin and the terms of the 1939 concession

stops.name: Roquebrune: the ossuary and the assembled skeleton
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and two stages that a research entry compressed into one. The remains went to the communal ossuary when the concession lapsed in 1946; the reassembly of a skeleton by a French doctor belongs to 1948, when the Irish request arrived and the authorities said they could no longer locate the actual remains. The account rests on a 2015 find in French diplomatic papers plus press reporting, and is disputed by the Yeats family.
stops.campa: When the concession lapses the bones go into the communal ossuary with everyone else's, which is ordinary practice in a French village and unremarkable until a government asks for one man back. In 1948 the authorities cannot produce him. A doctor is given the ossuary and assembles out of it a skeleton said to present all the characteristics of the deceased. The Irish minister does not ask how the collection was made. The poet's son, standing there, does not ask either.
suggested_refs: Declassified French diplomatic correspondence on the 1946 to 1948 exhumation, surfaced 2015
sources: Declassified French diplomatic correspondence cited in Wikipedia

stops.name: Drumcliff, St Columba's: Horseman, pass by
stops.date_confidence: the repatriation is attested to September 1948; the day, 17 September, comes from Foster and the press accounts. Coordinate follows the afterlife figure of 54.3308, -8.4936; a research figure of 54.3403, -8.4986 sits over a kilometre north of the churchyard.
stops.campa: The corvette Macha carries the coffin from the French coast to Galway and the state gives him a funeral with a naval escort and a government behind it. He is laid in the churchyard where his great-grandfather was rector, under the mountain that closed every horizon of his childhood, and the stone at his head is cut with the three lines he wrote for it in the last year of his life. Whether the bones beneath it are his has never been tested, and the state that buried them has not asked to test them.
stops.quote: Cast a cold Eye / On Life, on Death. / Horseman, pass by!
stops.quote_source: Yeats, epitaph composed in Under Ben Bulben (1938), inscribed at Drumcliff, 1948
suggested_refs: St Columba's churchyard, Drumcliff, Co. Sligo, and the LE Macha repatriation of September 1948
sources: Irish Naval Service records cited in press accounts

stops.name: Thoor Ballylee: the tower opened on the hundredth birthday
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, Thoor Ballylee): the Kiltartan Society was founded by Mary Hanley in 1961 and Padraic Colum opened the restored tower on 20 June 1965
stops.campa: Mary Hanley's Kiltartan Society, founded four years earlier to keep the memory of the writers of this one small barony, raises the money to reroof the tower, furnish it with first editions and period pieces, and open it as a museum; Padraic Colum unlocks the door on the twentieth of June, the hundredth birthday. The Streamstown river floods it again in 2009, and Storm Desmond hits it in the December after it reopens for the hundred and fiftieth. The stone by the door has outlasted every roof.
stops.quote: I, the poet William Yeats, / With old mill boards and sea-green slates, / And smithy work from the Gort forge, / Restored this tower for my wife George. / And may these characters remain / When all is ruin once again.
stops.quote_source: Inscription composed by Yeats and cut into a tablet at Thoor Ballylee
suggested_refs: The Yeats inscription tablet at Thoor Ballylee and the Kiltartan Society restoration of 1965
